title: What Is PDA Stylus? — Definition
body:
Mobile history before the smartphone: brick phones (DynaTAC), flip phones (StarTAC, RAZR), Nokia's candybar era, BlackBerry's keyboard, Palm Pilots and Windows CE PDAs, Apple's Newton, MP3 players (iPod, Zune), and the networks (AMPS, GSM, pagers) that carried them.

In the context of this database, the PDA Stylus is presented as one mobile history record among the mobile and pda history family. The plastic pen: the stylus's tap — the PDA's finger.

title: Origins and History of PDA Stylus
body:
The PDA Stylus belongs to the 1990s–2000s era and traces to Various.

Car phones (MTS, 1946) preceded cellular; Bell Labs' cellular concept waited for switching tech. Motorola's DynaTAC (1983, $3,995) made the handheld call; StarTAC (1996) made it pocketable. GSM (1991) digitized Europe; Nokia's 5110/3310 made the phone a fashion object with Snake. BlackBerry (1999/2002) put email in pockets; Palm Pilot (1996) proved the PDA; Apple's Newton (1993) overreached. The iPod (2001) taught Apple mobile; the 2007 iPhone ended this era — but the brick, the flip, and the clickwheel defined mobile culture first.

Within that longer story, PDA Stylus: The silo's storage; the Graffiti's strokes. The stylus is the PDA's pen.

title: How PDA Stylus Works
body:
1G (AMPS) carried analog voice in 30 kHz channels; 2G (GSM, cdmaOne) digitized it with TDMA/CDMA and added SMS (first sent 1992). Phones registered with the network via SIM (GSM) or burned-in ESN (AMPS/CDMA); base stations handed calls between cells. Pagers received one-way numeric/alphanumeric pages over POCSAG/FLEX at 900 MHz. PDAs synced via serial/IR cradles (HotSync); early smartphones ran Palm OS, Symbian, or Windows Mobile on ARM chips with resistive touchscreens and styli.

Applied to the PDA Stylus (1990s–2000s, Various): The stylus is the PDA's pen.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of PDA Stylus — Components
body:
Every PDA Stylus is an assembly of the mobile and pda history family's standard parts:

• Radio / baseband — Cellular transceiver; the phone's voice.
• Antenna — Stub, whip, then internal PIFA.
• SIM / ESN — Subscriber identity: card vs burned-in.
• Display — Monochrome LCD, then CSTN/TFT color.
• Keypad — 12-key + T9 predictive text.
• Battery — NiCd, NiMH, then Li-ion; the brick's bulk.
• Speaker / mic — Earpiece and microphone capsules.
• Vibrator motor — Silent alert; the pager legacy.
• Stylus & digitizer — Resistive touch on PDAs.
• Cradle / sync cable — Serial/USB HotSync to the desktop.

When examining a surviving PDA Stylus, identify these parts in order: Radio / baseband, Antenna, SIM / ESN, Display, Keypad, Battery.

title: Mobile and PDA History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of mobile and pda history:

• 1G / 2G — Analog cellular / digital cellular generations.
• AMPS — Advanced Mobile Phone System; the US 1G standard.
• GSM — Global System for Mobile; SIM cards and SMS.
• SMS — Short Message Service; 160 characters that changed the world.
• T9 — Predictive text on 12-key pads.
• POCSAG / FLEX — Pager protocols; one-way messaging.
• WAP — Wireless Application Protocol; the pre-web mobile web.
• HotSync — Palm's one-button desktop sync.
• Graffiti — Palm's stroke alphabet for stylus input.
• Symbian — The smartphone OS before the smartphone era.
• candybar / clamshell / slider — The three phone form factors.
• brick phone — DynaTAC-class handhelds; the original mobile.

title: PDA Stylus in Culture
body:
The brick was power; the StarTAC was cool; the Nokia 3310 is indestructible meme royalty. Texting created a language (c u l8r); Snake filled boring moments; polyphonic ringtones were identity. BlackBerry's click was the sound of business; the Palm's HotSync was a ritual. Pagers meant you were important — or on call.

The PDA Stylus carries that cultural charge directly: The stylus is the PDA's pen.

title: Collecting and Preserving PDA Stylus
body:
Boxed DynaTACs and StarTACs are grails; most need battery rebuilds (recell the packs). Nokia 3310s are plentiful — Xpress-on covers multiply. Newtons need capacitor work. iPods need batteries and often hard-drive-to-flash mods. Pagers are cheap and fun; they can't receive anymore, but they light up.

For the PDA Stylus specifically: The plastic pen: the stylus's tap — the PDA's finger.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working PDA Stylus with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: PDA Stylus Restoration Guide
body:
Recell battery packs (spot-weld, don't solder cells). Clean keypad contacts and charging ports. Replace backup capacitors in PDAs. Flash-mod iPods for reliability. Keep lithium cells at storage charge; never puncture.

Restoration order for a PDA Stylus: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical mobile history record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: PDA Stylus — T9 predictive text + SMS segmenter (Runnable Python)
body:
Implements T9 keypress-to-word prediction on a classic 12-key pad and computes SMS segmentation — the two defining algorithms of the keypad era.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the PDA Stylus so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# T9 predictive text + SMS segmentation (public-domain concepts)
KEYS = {"2":"abc","3":"def","4":"ghi","5":"jkl","6":"mno",
        "7":"pqrs","8":"tuv","9":"wxyz"}
WORDS = ["hello","good","home","gone","hood","call","ball","apple",
         "how","are","you","me","the","and","test","text"]

def t9(keys):
    out = []
    for w in WORDS:
        if len(w) != len(keys): continue
        if all(ch in KEYS[k] for ch, k in zip(w, keys)):
            out.append(w)
    return out

print("4663 ->", t9("4663"))   # hello / good / home / gone / hood
print("2255 ->", t9("2255"))   # call / ball

# SMS: 160 GSM-7 chars single, 153 per segment concatenated
def sms_segments(text):
    n = len(text)
    if n <= 160: return 1, n
    import math
    segs = math.ceil(n / 153)
    return segs, n
for msg in ["see you at 8", "x" * 200]:
    s, n = sms_segments(msg)
    print(f"{n} chars -> {s} segment(s)")
